title: The pro-rata rule (with a $90,000 example)

concepts.title: What the pro-rata rule does
concepts.body: The pro-rata rule says: when you convert a traditional IRA to a Roth, the IRS treats the conversion as a proportional mix of pre-tax and after-tax money — based on your aggregate IRA balances on December 31 of the conversion year. It does not look at the specific account you convert.

concepts.title: The $90,000 example
concepts.body: Say you have $90,000 in a pre-tax traditional IRA. You contribute $7,000 after-tax to a second traditional IRA, then convert the $7,000 to a Roth. Under the pro-rata rule, the $7,000 conversion is 7/97 pre-tax and 7,000/97,000 = ~7.2% pre-tax — the rest is taxable. Of the $7,000 converted, about $7,000 × (90,000/97,000) = $6,495 is taxable as ordinary income. The 'non-deductible' part vanishes.

concepts.title: The fix: roll the pre-tax balance to a 401(k) first
concepts.body: Move the $90,000 pre-tax IRA into your 401(k) — if the plan accepts rollovers. Now your only IRA is the new $7,000 after-tax one. The pro-rata aggregation finds zero pre-tax, and the entire $7,000 conversion is tax-free. The backdoor Roth works as advertised.

sources: IRS — IRC §408(d)(2) — Nondeductible Traditional IRA contributions and Roth conversions
IRS Pub 590-A — Backdoor Roth IRA strategy and pro-rata aggregation
